note: Legal-safety layer. This skill deliberately NEVER emits artist names, studio names, franchise names or brand names in prompts. Two reasons: (1) some engines refuse or throttle prompts naming living artists or studios, (2) naming a studio to imitate its output is legally risky for a redistributable skill. Use the right-hand generic descriptors instead.
policy: Never write 'in the style of <artist>', '<artist>-style', 'like <movie/TV/game character>'.
Describe the visual FEATURE you want, not the name of the thing that has it.

Generic descriptors are safe to state plainly, including: cel shaded, flat vector, low poly, voxel, pixel art, matte 3D render, soft clay, needle felt, oil impasto, watercolour, gouache, risograph print, linocut, art deco poster, mid-century modern poster, comic book ink, studio Ghibli-style -> replace with 'painterly Japanese animation background art with lush hand-painted landscape detail'.
Product brands: never name a real brand. Say 'a red aluminium soda can', 'a yellow banana-shaped phone case' instead.
Franchise characters: never name them. Say 'a small round mouse with big round ears and red shorts' instead.
If a user insists on a named artist, explain the tradeoff once, then comply with the generic-descriptor rewrite instead of the name.

Pixar-style 3D: soft matte 3D render with expressive eyes
cute style: cute stylised character with large eyes and soft forms
cinematic look: cinematic lighting with shallow depth of field
minimalist: minimal flat design with generous negative space
corporate friendly: clean flat illustration with a soft palette
watercolor: watercolour with wet edges and granulation

risk_notes: Avoid 'in the style of' entirely; some engines block it.
Avoid the words Pixar, Disney, Ghibli, Mario, Pokemon, LEGO, Sanrio, Marvel in prompts - they trigger filters and are legally risky.
Do not request real celebrity likenesses.
Do not request real brand logos or product packaging; describe generic products instead.
If your channel produces commercial work, check the target engine's terms about artist-style references before publishing prompts publicly.
